summary: Waukegan's cast-iron pier light, first shown 31 August 1899 at the end of the south pier, replaced a bluff light; a 1913 rescue and a 1967 fire mark its later years.

structures.note: About 35 feet (10.7 m) from base to ventilator ball (Pepper); lantern removed after the 1967 fire.
Standing; recently used for commercial purposes (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Visitors walk out the pier to the tower (Pepper).

events.note: First shown on the south-pier tower 31 August 1899; a temporary north-pier light had been shown from 10 August 1898.
Cast-iron tower erected 36 feet from the outer end of the south pier.
Tower moved to the end of the pier extension (about 1,400 feet); relit 7 February 1905.
Two-story fog-signal building attached; sirens ran 442 hours in the first year (Pepper).
Head keeper Frederick W. Raether fell from the icy pier in December 1907; his body was found more than a year later (LighthouseFriends).
Double keepers' dwelling built on shore.
Assistant keeper Emil C. Tews rescued Wallace R. Sunderlin from Lake Michigan on 9 November 1913.
Tower electrified; new fog signal installed.
Fire on 1 June 1967 destroyed the fog-signal building and the lantern room. Cause: electrical short (LighthouseFriends); undetermined (Pepper).
Army Corps of Engineers renovated the lighthouse pier; now wheelchair accessible.

corrections.why: The Board's FY1900 report says the iron tower was erected 36 feet from the outer end of the south pier and lit 31 August 1899. No primary source for an 1889 tower was found; Pepper's page has an 1889 date that is evidently 1898.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record, Wikipedia's lead and the Rowlett-based events give 1889. The Board's FY1899 and FY1900 reports, LighthouseFriends and Pepper describe a permanent metal tower erected in 1899 at the end of the south pier, preceded by a 1898 post light on the north pier. The story follows the 1899 reports.

The FY1899 report describes a contract for the north pier but a foundation at the end of the south pier. The FY1900 report and LighthouseFriends place the tower on the south pier, which the 1905 move at the pier extension confirms.

notes_for_editor: (1) Tower date: the record, Wikipedia's lead and Rowlett-based events say 1889; the Board's reports say a metal tower was erected in 1899 (corrected in corrections). No primary 1889 source was found. (2) Owner: the record says unknown; Wikipedia's lead says the Coast Guard, but no Light List entry was read, so ownership is left out of the JSON. (3) 'Active Aid to Navigation? No' in the USLHS record conflicts with the record's status 'active' and with LighthouseFriends' description of a displayed light. Not resolved. (4) Characteristic: the record gives Oc G 4s from the chart data; the sources read give only 'occulting green' and no period, so the JSON uses characteristic_today. (5) Fog signal (1906): LighthouseFriends describes a two-story building with two mineral-oil engines producing a horn blast; Pepper describes compressed-air sirens with diesel compressors. Not resolved. (6) 1967 fire cause: electrical short (LighthouseFriends) against undetermined (Pepper). Both are cited. (7) Two first assistants named Dues (Peter Dues head keeper 1899-1902; Peter H. Dues first assistant 1899-1903) are not linked; no source connects them. (8) The Little Fort bluff light is a separate USLHS record (little-fort-waukegan) with keepers from 1849 to 1899. Only its first keeper is named in the story. (9) Part of the Board's FY1899 text is OCR-damaged (north-pier paragraph); quotations are limited to clean passages, and the north-pier contract is paraphrased. (10) Pepper's page has date slips (1889 for 1898; 'the following year' for the tower erection); the story uses the Board's dates. (11) The USLHS place record gives 42 deg 21 min 39 sec N, 87 deg 49 min 13 sec W, about 0.6 km west of the record's position (which agrees with Wikipedia's coordinates). Not corrected: the USLHS figure is minute-level. (12) Carnegie gives Tews's age as 43 and calls him 'assistant lighthouse keeper'; the Bulletin calls him 'first assistant keeper'. (13) The roster lines are printed as the archive gives them. Keepers whose service ended after about 1960 are not named in the story. (14) No photos were added; the record's Commons photo has no licence information in the record. (15) Fog-signal disagreement is now stated in the text: LighthouseFriends describes a fog horn driven by two mineral-oil engines; Pepper describes compressed-air sirens with diesel compressors. The 442 hours are Pepper's figure. (16) The 1913 rescue: the Carnegie record says Sunderlin went out 'during a storm'; the story uses 'storm' (LighthouseFriends quotes Tews calling it 'the gale'). (17) The phrase 'the opening into the harbor' for the north-breakwater light is Pepper's (fact-check 2026-10-28). (18) The story no longer says the bluff stood 'above the lake'; the sources say only 'on the bluff'.
